title: Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge
audience: Owners of small Australian property trade businesses who need a base rate and a minimum charge before quoting
learningOutcomes: Separate billable hours from non-billable hours, and calculate the time available to bill.
Calculate a base hourly rate from the owner's own costs and income target, then compare it with local evidence.
Set a minimum charge for short jobs, and explain it to a client before the visit.

instruction.heading: Factors that move the rate
instruction.body: A rate depends on skill, experience, how scarce the skill is locally, the range of work offered and the cost of running the business. An owner who offers several services that a client can book in one visit may justify a higher rate, because the client saves time. A narrow range of basic tasks in a crowded market may need a rate closer to local norms. Experience matters too. A new business should price honestly and review the rate regularly, rather than cutting it to win work. Use the local evidence from “Choosing your service list and checking local demand”, “Finding local customers without relying on bidding sites” and “Online job platforms: choosing and setting up a profile”, not a published national average. The guide this lesson draws on gives a US national average, and that figure is not used here.

instruction.heading: Counting the hours that can be billed
instruction.body: Owners often price as though every hour of the week can be billed. Few can. Travel, quoting, admin, marketing, training, equipment upkeep, sick days and leave are not billable. Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract the non-billable time to reach billable hours. If only part of the paid time can be billed, the rate must be higher than it would be if every hour could be billed. For example, if sixty of every hundred paid hours are billable, the costs of all one hundred hours must be recovered from the sixty, so the rate is about 1.67 times the rate needed for a fully billable week. A Jobber guide puts billable time at about 60 to 80 percent of working hours. That is a general range rather than an Australian figure, so check your own log against it.

instruction.heading: Building the rate from costs and income
instruction.body: Add the annual costs of running the business, including insurance, registration, equipment and its upkeep, the vehicle, phone, software, marketing and accounting, to the income needed to live on. A business.gov.au pricing guide says on-costs such as superannuation, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure, so decide how each will be allowed for. Have a registered tax agent confirm how leave and superannuation are treated for the owner's situation before the rate is published. Divide the total by the billable hours to reach the base rate. A personal-training pricing guide from AIPT works backwards from a target income, dividing by working weeks and then by weekly hours, with tax and business costs added on top. Its example figures are not used here. Review the base rate each quarter, and compare it with what clients accept and with the local evidence.

instruction.heading: Setting a minimum charge for short jobs
instruction.body: Short jobs can cost more in time than they earn, because travel and setup do not shrink with the size of the task. A minimum charge or a call-out fee covers the time needed to attend the site and start work. Set the minimum so that a short job still covers travel, setup and admin. State it before the visit, and explain it to the client in plain terms. A contractor pricing guide suggests setting the minimum from the full cost of the visit, dividing that cost by one minus the target margin, with the minimum covering travel, setup and cleanup. Its figures are labelled illustrative and are not used here.

procedure: Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract travel, admin, marketing, training and leave to find the billable hours.
List the annual running costs, including insurance, registration, equipment, vehicle, phone, software and marketing.
Add the income needed, including allowances for leave and tax confirmed by a registered tax agent.
Divide the total by the billable hours to find the base rate.
Set a minimum charge that covers travel, setup and admin for a short job, and state it in writing.
Review the rate each quarter, and record any change and the reason for it.

workedExamples.situation: An owner's calculation shows that only sixty of every hundred paid hours can be billed, but the owner plans to set the rate as if every paid hour could be billed.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the effect on the rate if the wrong assumption is kept?
workedExamples.reasoning: Pricing as if every paid hour were billable understates the rate, because the costs and the income still have to come out of the hours that can be billed. The rate must be built from billable hours, then checked against the local evidence and the minimum charge before it is published.

equipmentAndPpe: Log of paid and billable hours for one month
Price sheet with the base rate and the minimum charge

commonErrors.error: Setting a rate from a published average or a competitor's figure without checking the costs.
commonErrors.prevention: Build the base rate from the owner's own costs and billable hours, then compare it with local evidence.

commonErrors.error: Pricing as though every paid hour could be billed.
commonErrors.prevention: Subtract the non-billable time before dividing.

commonErrors.error: Taking short jobs at the same rate, without covering travel and setup.
commonErrors.prevention: Set and state a minimum charge that covers travel, setup and admin.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Price display rules come from the Australian Consumer Law, as summarised in the ACCC guide in R1. That guide does not cover minimum or call-out charges, or what counts as a fair term. Check those points against current ACCC guidance or a legal adviser before publishing a price sheet.
Confirm it with a registered tax agent.

qualityStandard: Billable hours are calculated from a logged or estimated month, not assumed.
The base rate is built from the owner's costs and income target, and is compared with local evidence.
A minimum charge is set and stated before any short job.
documentationEvidence: Annual costs and income worksheet, with the source and date of each cost
Billable hours calculation showing the non-billable deductions
Price sheet showing the base rate, the minimum charge and the review date
summary: Price from billable hours, not from paid hours.
Build the rate from costs and a stated income target, then check it against local evidence.
Set and state a minimum charge for short jobs.

knowledgeChecks.question: An owner can bill only some of the paid hours. How should the rate be built?
options: From all paid hours, so the rate looks lower and so the client pays less per job
From billable hours, so the costs and income are covered by the work that can be billed
From the average published on a website and from the rate listed by the nearest competitor
From the rate the owner wishes the market would pay and the owner's own mood on the day

knowledgeChecks.question: Why set a minimum charge for short jobs?
options: Because short jobs need travel but no setup time at all and the admin takes no time
Because travel, setup and admin time does not shrink with the size of the job
Because clients expect every job to cost the same amount, whatever its size
Because a minimum charge replaces a written quote for every job the owner takes

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best source for checking a base hourly rate?
options: A single published national average from the largest trade body
The owner's own costs and billable hours, compared with local evidence
A friend's rate, without checking the costs or the local market
The rate shown on the first page of a bidding site this week

Tactic (team4 hourly-rate research): add on-costs such as super, leave and tax to the hourly figure. Source: business.gov.au, 'Choose a pricing strategy', https://business.gov.au/products-and-services/choose-a-pricing-strategy, 1 October 2026 (page metadata).

Tactic (team4 pricing-hours research and hourly-rate research): billable time about 60 to 80 percent of working hours. Source: Jobber, 'What are billable hours', https://getjobber.com/academy/what-are-billable-hours/, published 5 November 2024, last modified 20 July 2026. General range, not an Australian figure.

Tactic (team4 hourly-rate research): work backwards from a target income. Source: AIPT, 'Personal Training Prices: Setting the Right Rates', https://www.aipt.edu.au/articles/personal-training-prices-how-much-should-you-charge, 16 May 2025. Example figures not used.

Tactic (team4 hourly-rate research): minimum set from full visit cost with a margin, and the minimum covering travel, setup and admin. Source: Contractor+, 'Minimum Service Call Charge: A Contractor's Pricing Guide', https://contractorplus.app/blog/minimum-service-call-charge, 23 September 2026. Source labels its figures illustrative; not used.

Tactic (team4 hourly-rate research): review the price about every three months. Source: Business Victoria, 'Develop a pricing strategy', https://business.vic.gov.au/business-information/finance/pricing-for-profit/develop-a-pricing-strategy, no date shown on page.

officialReferences.title: Advertising and selling guide: A guide for business
officialReferences.covers: Says a single advertised price should state the total price and include any tax, duty, fee, levy or other additional charges. Does not address minimum or call-out charges, or tax on leave and superannuation, which remain UNCONFIRMED. The guide is dated July 2021, so confirm it is still current before use. Publisher: ACCC.
